title: The Saints and the Dead
lead: Are believers who have died still joined to the church on earth? The Apostles' Creed confesses "the communion of saints," but churches differ on whether the saints in heaven pray for us, whether we may ask them to, whether their relics should be honored, and whether the living should pray for the dead.

sections.h: The dead in the Old Testament
sections.b: The law forbids consulting the dead, along with fortune-tellers and mediums (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). King Saul broke this rule when he had a medium at Endor call up the prophet Samuel, and Samuel announced his doom (1 Samuel 28:3–19). Yet a dead man came back to life when his body touched the bones of Elisha (2 Kings 13:21). Most of the Old Testament pictures the dead as gone down to Sheol, the place of the dead, where they cannot praise God (Psalm 6:5; Psalm 88:10–12). In 2 Maccabees, a book in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, Judas Maccabeus has an offering made for fallen soldiers so they might be freed from their sin (2 Maccabees 12:43–46).
sections.refs: Deuteronomy 18:10–12; 1 Samuel 28:3–19; 2 Kings 13:21; Psalm 6:5; Psalm 88:10–12; 2 Maccabees 12:43–46

sections.h: The saints in the New Testament
sections.b: In the New Testament, "saints" means all of God's holy people, living or dead (Romans 1:7). Jesus says God is the God of the living, "for to him all are alive" (Luke 20:38), and Moses and Elijah talk with Jesus on the mountain (Mark 9:4). Hebrews pictures a "great cloud of witnesses" around the church (Hebrews 12:1). In Revelation the elders hold "gold bowls full of incense. These are the prayers of the saints" (Revelation 5:8), and the souls under the altar cry out to God (Revelation 6:9–10). Handkerchiefs that had touched Paul healed the sick (Acts 19:11–12). Believers are told to pray for one another (James 5:16), and Paul's wish that the Lord show mercy to Onesiphorus, who may have died, is read by some as a prayer for the dead (2 Timothy 1:16–18).
sections.refs: Romans 1:7; Luke 20:38; Mark 9:4; Hebrews 12:1; Revelation 5:8; Revelation 6:9–10; Revelation 8:3–4; Acts 19:11–12; James 5:16; 2 Timothy 1:16–18

sections.b: Catholic and Orthodox Christians teach that death does not break the bond of love in Christ's body. The saints in heaven pray for the church, and believers may ask them to, just as they ask a friend on earth. Both churches honor the relics, the bodies or belongings, of saints, citing Elisha's bones and Paul's handkerchiefs, and both pray for the dead. They say this honor (Greek dulia) differs from the worship (latreia) owed to God alone, and that asking the saints for prayer is not the consulting of the dead that the law forbids. Catholic teaching adds purgatory, a final cleansing after death for those who die in God's grace but are not yet fully purified. Orthodox churches pray for the departed without defining purgatory.
sections.refs: 2 Kings 13:21; Acts 19:11–12; Revelation 5:8; Hebrews 12:1; 1 Corinthians 3:13–15; 2 Maccabees 12:43–46

sections.b: The Lutheran Augsburg Confession says the saints should be remembered so that believers may follow their faith and good works, but that Scripture does not teach calling on them for help, since Christ is the one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5). Reformed, Baptist, Pentecostal and most evangelical churches agree and do not pray to saints, honor relics or pray for the dead. They read the law against consulting the dead as a warning, and say Revelation's prayers in bowls describe worship in heaven, not a pattern for the church. The Anglican Thirty-Nine Articles reject purgatory and the invoking of saints, though some Anglo-Catholics practice both. Adventists and Jehovah's Witnesses teach that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection, so they can neither hear nor pray.

common: Christians agree that believers on earth should pray for one another and remember the faithful who have gone before.
uncommon: A few Protestant writers accept that the saints in heaven pray for the church in general, while still refusing to ask them for prayer.
